sources.entry: Why you should use links, not keys, to represent relationships in APIs, Martin Nally, Google

summary.title: API links vs keys: Why you should use links, not keys, to represent relationships in APIs
summary.one_liner: Web APIs should expose relationships between resources as HTTP URL links rather than database foreign keys, which reduces client-server coupling and the documentation clients must learn.
takeaways: Represent relationships with URL links (with a relation name) instead of database keys, so clients don't need to compose URLs from keys.
Links reduce the number of URI templates a provider must document and a client must learn, and let the server change URL formats freely.
Caveats include reverse-proxy URL rewriting, API versioning in URLs (use links to unversioned URLs), and documenting templates for PUT or query support.
Use a nested object style such as {"owner": {"self": "/people/98765"}} to make clear the value is a URL, and use a standard 'self' name.
summary.summary: Martin Nally, a Google API designer, argues that APIs should represent entity relationships with links based on HTTP URLs rather than foreign keys. He walks through a pet store example, comparing a key-based design (with many URI templates) to a link-based one, and explains the benefits for coupling and documentation. The post also covers caveats such as proxy URL rewriting, versioning, PUT-based creation, query URLs, and JSON link styles.
